Introduction

In the digital age, data is one of the most valuable resources for understanding organizational dynamics and driving decision-making. This project takes a deep dive into analyzing an employee dataset using Python to uncover meaningful insights such as performance trends, salary distributions, hiring patterns, and more. By following this tutorial, readers will learn how to apply Python's data analysis and visualization tools to real-world data.

Lessons to Learn

This project demonstrates how to:

  • Analyze performance trends across departments.
  • Visualize salary distributions and correlate them with performance.
  • Understand hiring trends and tenure patterns.
  • Leverage data to uncover actionable insights for organizational improvement.

Key Concepts Used

This tutorial applies the following Python techniques and libraries:

  1. Data Manipulation: Using Pandas to clean and organize data.
  2. Visualization: Employing Matplotlib and Seaborn for insightful visual representations.
  3. Statistics: Analyzing correlations and averages to derive insights.
  4. Time-Series Analysis: Tracking trends over time to identify patterns.

Dataset Overview

The dataset used in this project includes fields such as:

  • Department: Employee's department.
  • Performance_Score: Employee's performance rating.
  • Salary: Employee salary.
  • City: City where the employee works.
  • Join_Date: Date the employee joined.
  • Age: Employee age.

These columns provide a comprehensive view of employee demographics, financials, and performance metrics.

Inputs and Steps Explained

The inputs are straightforward and include the employee dataset saved as an Excel file (employee_dataset.xlsx). Below is an overview of the key analyses performed:

employee_datasetDownload

1. Department Performance Analysis

This analysis computes the average performance score for each department.

Code Example:

def department_performance_analysis(df: DataFrame):
    """
    This method analyze average performance scores across departments
    :param df:
    :return:
    """
    performance_summary: DataFrame = (
        df.groupby('Department')['Performance_Score']
        .mean()
        .reset_index()
        .rename(columns={'Performance_Score': 'Avg_Performance_Score'})
        .sort_values(by='Avg_Performance_Score', ascending=False)
    )
    print("Average Performance Scores by Department:")
    print(performance_summary)
    return performance_summary

2. Salary Pivot Table

Generates a pivot table to analyze salary distribution by city and department.

Code Example:

def salary_pivot_table(df: DataFrame):
    salary_pivot: DataFrame = pd.pivot_table(
        df,
        values='Salary',
        index='City',
        columns='Department',
        aggfunc='mean'
    )
    print("Salary Distribution by City and Department:")
    print(salary_pivot)
    return salary_pivot

3. Hiring Trends Analysis

Tracks hiring trends over time using a time-series analysis.

Code Example:

def hiring_trend_analysis(df: DataFrame):
    """
    Time-series analysis of hiring trends
    :param df:
    """
    df['Join_Year'] = df['Join_Date'].dt.year
    hiring_trend = df.groupby('Join_Year').size()
    print("Hiring Trend Over the Years:")
    print(hiring_trend)

    # Plotting the trend
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    sns.lineplot(x=hiring_trend.index, y=hiring_trend.values, marker='o')
    plt.title("Hiring Trends (2010-2023)")
    plt.xlabel("Year")
    plt.ylabel("Number of Hires")
    plt.grid(True)
    plt.show()

4. Average Salary by Age Group

Groups employees into age ranges and calculates the average salary for each group.

Code Example:

def average_salary_by_age_group(df):
    bins = [20, 30, 40, 50, 60]
    labels = ['20-29', '30-39', '40-49', '50-59']
    df['Age_Group'] = pd.cut(df['Age'], bins=bins, labels=labels, right=False)
    age_salary_summary = (
        df.groupby('Age_Group',  observed=False)['Salary']
        .mean()
        .reset_index()
        .rename(columns={'Salary': 'Avg_Salary'})
    )
    print("Average Salary by Age Group:")
    print(age_salary_summary)
    return age_salary_summary

5. Top Cities By Performance

This gives us the cities with the best performance

Code Example:

def top_cities_by_performance(df: DataFrame):
    city_performance = (
        df.groupby('City')['Performance_Score']
        .mean()
        .reset_index()
        .rename(columns={'Performance_Score': 'Avg_Performance_Score'})
        .sort_values(by='Avg_Performance_Score', ascending=False)
        .head(5)
    )
    print("Top 5 Cities by Average Performance Score:")
    print(city_performance)
    return city_performance

Full Code

For readers to follow along, here's the complete code for the project. Copy and paste this into your Python environment:

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from pandas import DataFrame

# Load the dataset
file_path: str = "employee_dataset.xlsx"
df: DataFrame = pd.read_excel(file_path)


# 1. Analyze average performance scores across departments
def department_performance_analysis(df: DataFrame):
    """
    This method analyze average performance scores across departments
    :param df:
    :return:
    """
    performance_summary: DataFrame = (
        df.groupby('Department')['Performance_Score']
        .mean()
        .reset_index()
        .rename(columns={'Performance_Score': 'Avg_Performance_Score'})
        .sort_values(by='Avg_Performance_Score', ascending=False)
    )
    print("Average Performance Scores by Department:")
    print(performance_summary)
    return performance_summary


# 2. Generate pivot table for salary distribution by city and department
def salary_pivot_table(df: DataFrame):
    salary_pivot: DataFrame = pd.pivot_table(
        df,
        values='Salary',
        index='City',
        columns='Department',
        aggfunc='mean'
    )
    print("Salary Distribution by City and Department:")
    print(salary_pivot)
    return salary_pivot


# 3. Time-series analysis of hiring trends
def hiring_trend_analysis(df: DataFrame):
    """
    Time-series analysis of hiring trends
    :param df:
    """
    df['Join_Year'] = df['Join_Date'].dt.year
    hiring_trend = df.groupby('Join_Year').size()
    print("Hiring Trend Over the Years:")
    print(hiring_trend)

    # Plotting the trend
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    sns.lineplot(x=hiring_trend.index, y=hiring_trend.values, marker='o')
    plt.title("Hiring Trends (2010-2023)")
    plt.xlabel("Year")
    plt.ylabel("Number of Hires")
    plt.grid(True)
    plt.show()


# 4. Analyze the average salary by age group
def average_salary_by_age_group(df):
    bins = [20, 30, 40, 50, 60]
    labels = ['20-29', '30-39', '40-49', '50-59']
    df['Age_Group'] = pd.cut(df['Age'], bins=bins, labels=labels, right=False)
    age_salary_summary = (
        df.groupby('Age_Group',  observed=False)['Salary']
        .mean()
        .reset_index()
        .rename(columns={'Salary': 'Avg_Salary'})
    )
    print("Average Salary by Age Group:")
    print(age_salary_summary)
    return age_salary_summary


# 5. Identify the top 5 cities with the highest average performance scores
def top_cities_by_performance(df: DataFrame):
    city_performance = (
        df.groupby('City')['Performance_Score']
        .mean()
        .reset_index()
        .rename(columns={'Performance_Score': 'Avg_Performance_Score'})
        .sort_values(by='Avg_Performance_Score', ascending=False)
        .head(5)
    )
    print("Top 5 Cities by Average Performance Score:")
    print(city_performance)
    return city_performance


# 6. Analyze salary distribution by age using boxplots
def salary_distribution_by_age(df):
    """
    Analyze salary distribution by age using boxplots
    :param df:
    """
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    sns.boxplot(x='Age', y='Salary', data=df)
    plt.title("Salary Distribution by Age")
    plt.xlabel("Age")
    plt.ylabel("Salary")
    plt.show()


# 7. Find the department with the longest average tenure of employees
def longest_tenure_by_department(df):
    df['Tenure'] = (pd.Timestamp.now() - df['Join_Date']).dt.days / 365
    tenure_summary = (
        df.groupby('Department')['Tenure']
        .mean()
        .reset_index()
        .rename(columns={'Tenure': 'Avg_Tenure'})
        .sort_values(by='Avg_Tenure', ascending=False)
    )
    print("Longest Average Tenure by Department:")
    print(tenure_summary)
    return tenure_summary


# 8. Correlate performance scores with salaries to identify trends
def performance_salary_correlation(df):
    correlation = df['Performance_Score'].corr(df['Salary'])
    print(f"Correlation between Performance Score and Salary: {correlation:.2f}")

    # Scatter plot
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    sns.scatterplot(x='Performance_Score', y='Salary', data=df)
    plt.title("Correlation Between Performance Score and Salary")
    plt.xlabel("Performance Score")
    plt.ylabel("Salary")
    plt.show()


# 9. Visualize department size as a percentage of total employees
def department_size_visualization(df):
    department_counts = df['Department'].value_counts(normalize=True) * 100
    department_counts.plot(kind='pie', autopct='%1.1f%%', figsize=(8, 8))
    plt.title("Department Size as Percentage of Total Employees")
    plt.ylabel("")
    plt.show()


# 10. Analyze hiring trends by city over the years
def hiring_trend_by_city(df):
    df['Join_Year'] = df['Join_Date'].dt.year
    hiring_trends = (
        df.groupby(['City', 'Join_Year']).size()
        .reset_index(name='Hires')
        .pivot(index='Join_Year', columns='City', values='Hires')
    )
    print("Hiring Trends by City Over the Years:")
    print(hiring_trends)

    # Plotting
    hiring_trends.plot(figsize=(12, 8))
    plt.title("Hiring Trends by City Over the Years")
    plt.xlabel("Year")
    plt.ylabel("Number of Hires")
    plt.legend(title="City", bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1), loc='upper left')
    plt.grid(True)
    plt.show()


# Combining analyses into a comprehensive report
def generate_report(df: DataFrame):
    print("Generating report...")

    print("1) Department Performance Analysis")
    department_performance = department_performance_analysis(df)

    print("2) Salary Pivot Table")
    salary_pivot = salary_pivot_table(df)

    print("3) Time-series analysis of hiring trends")
    hiring_trend_analysis(df)

    print("4) Average Salary by Age Group:")
    average_salary_by_age_group(df)

    print("5) Top Cities by Performance:")
    top_cities_by_performance(df)

    print("6) Salary Distribution by Age:")
    salary_distribution_by_age(df)

    print("7) Longest Tenure by Department:")
    longest_tenure_by_department(df)

    print("8) Performance and Salary Correlation:")
    performance_salary_correlation(df)

    print("9) Department Size Visualization:")
    department_size_visualization(df)

    print("10) Hiring Trends by City:")
    hiring_trend_by_city(df)

    return {}
    # return {
    #     "department_performance": department_performance,
    #     "salary_pivot": salary_pivot
    # }


# Example Use Cases
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Run all analyses
    report = generate_report(df)

Conclusion

This project highlights the power of Python for business analytics and demonstrates how data-driven insights can be generated from employee records. From performance evaluations to salary trends and hiring patterns, these analyses equip organizations with actionable knowledge.
